slides.title: Geometric Priors: Domains, Symmetries, Stability
slides.notes: Open by telling the room that this chapter is the hinge between generic high-dimensional learning and geometric deep learning. The lecture will not start with a layer name. It starts by asking what object indexes the data, which transformations are semantics-preserving, and what a model should do when those transformations are applied.

slides.title: The First Prior Is Where Values Live
slides.notes: Use this slide to slow down the basic vocabulary. A grid, graph, point cloud, and surface do not merely store values in different file formats. They define different neighborhoods and admissible coordinate changes, so the same vector of numbers can demand different models depending on its domain.

slides.title: A Transformation Of The Domain Induces One On Signals
slides.notes: Keep the triangle deliberately small. The point is not that every domain is triangular, but that a concrete action exposes the bookkeeping. Once the domain points move, signal coordinates must be pulled back so the same physical information is described after the transformation. That pullback is the representation.

slides.title: The Prior Lives Between Three Spaces
slides.notes: Frame this as the chapter's main diagrammatic habit. The same group can be discussed at three levels: it acts on the physical domain, it induces a representation on signal coordinates, and it restricts the functions we are willing to learn. This is why priors become statistical help rather than decorative terminology.

slides.title: Two Commuting Claims, Two Output Types
slides.notes: Ask students to read each square along both paths. For invariance, the right vertical edge is intentionally idle: transforming the input should not change a scalar decision. For equivariance, both vertical edges are active: the output is still a signal on a domain, so it must transform in step with the input.

slides.title: Adding Structure Shrinks The Symmetry Group
slides.notes: Use the relabeling picture to separate isomorphism from automorphism. An isomorphism may compare two differently named copies of the same structure. An automorphism maps a structure back to itself. This distinction is essential for graph learning, because node names are rarely semantic while adjacency usually is.

slides.title: Exact Symmetry Is Too Brittle For Real Data
slides.notes: Explain why the ring is not a new symmetry group. Small deformations compose into larger deformations, so closure fails if we only keep the small ones. The move is to measure distance from the exact group and ask for a Lipschitz-like response, which is a softer and more realistic geometric prior.

slides.title: Sometimes The Domain Moves, Not Just The Signal
slides.notes: Distinguish two stability settings. If only the signal changes, we can keep the domain fixed and use the representation of a deformation. If the graph, mesh, or manifold itself changes, the model needs a way to compare outputs across domains. That comparison is often where geometry enters most concretely.

slides.title: Local Computation Becomes Global Information
slides.notes: Connect this picture to the computational reason deep architectures help. Local neighborhoods are cheaper and more stable than arbitrary global interactions, but the task may require long-range information. Coarsening and composition let a model grow its receptive field while carrying forward the geometric constraints established at fine scale.

slides.title: Local Features Are A Stability Mechanism
slides.notes: Treat this as intuition rather than a theorem proof. The point is that global coordinates can make a tiny warp look like a complicated change everywhere, while local multiscale measurements compare nearby structure first. This is why geometric deep learning often combines local equivariant maps with pooling instead of jumping straight to a global invariant.

slides.title: The Blueprint: Local Equivariance, Coarsening, Invariant Readout
slides.notes: Present the blueprint as a design pattern rather than a single architecture. CNNs, GNNs, group networks, and manifold networks differ in their domains and representations, but the scaffold is recognizable: local equivariant processing, optional coarsening, and a final invariant decision when the task demands a coordinate-free output.

slides.title: The Notebook Turns Claims Into Residuals
slides.notes: Use this slide to model scientific hygiene. The lecture has used diagrams and formulas, but the notebook also records finite checks. A residual of zero on a toy convolution does not prove every network theorem; it verifies the exact mechanism being taught and gives students a pattern for debugging their own architecture claims.

slides.title: Break One Assumption And Predict The Failure
slides.notes: Make the exercise predictive, not just experimental. Students should first name the intended prior, then name the residual, then decide what should happen when an assumption is broken. If they cannot predict the failure mode, they probably have not yet separated invariance, equivariance, stability, and locality in their own model.

slides.title: Geometric Priors Are Design Contracts
slides.notes: Close by returning to the design contract language. A geometric prior is useful only when it identifies the right domain, the right transformation group or deformation family, and the right output behavior. The chapter's vocabulary is therefore practical: it tells us what to build, what to test, and when a popular architecture is the wrong match.
